sub.en: General ability, or one particular occasion? That is the choice.

items.q: She ___ swim before she could walk.
items.why: could = general ability over a period of time.

items.q: The water was freezing, but she ___ swim to the boat.
items.why: For one specific occasion in the positive, use was/were able to, not could.

items.q: It took four attempts, but he ___ pass the test.
items.why: manage to = it was difficult and you did it anyway.

items.q: After six months she ___ getting the job she wanted.
items.why: succeed in + -ing. It never takes an infinitive.

items.q: I ___ the temptation for about ten minutes, and then I gave in.
items.why: manage to = it was hard and you did it — here, for ten minutes. On one specific occasion could is not used in the positive.

items.q: They tried all afternoon, but they ___ open the door.
items.why: In the negative, couldn’t works for both general and specific ability.

acts.title: One night, four ways to say it
steps: can / could — general ability, no particular occasion
That night she was able to swim to the boat.
be able to — one specific occasion, positive
That night she managed to swim to the boat.
manage to — the same event, but it was hard
That night she succeeded in swimming to the boat.
succeed in + -ing — more formal, note the -ing
The others couldn’t swim that far.
couldn’t — the negative covers both meanings

acts.title: The marshmallow test
text: In the late 1960s a professor at Stanford University, Walter Mischel, put a marshmallow in front of a four-year-old and left the room. The child was told that he could eat it immediately, or, if he was able to wait until the researcher came back, he could have two as a reward. Then the researchers filmed what happened.

Fifteen minutes is a long time when you are four. Nearly seventy per cent of the children gave in. Some ate the marshmallow as soon as the door closed; others managed to wait a few minutes before temptation beat them. Only about thirty per cent succeeded in waiting the full fifteen minutes.

That result was not particularly surprising. What came later was. Years afterwards the researchers contacted the same children, who were now adults. The ones who had been able to wait had done better at school, earned more and reported better relationships. The ones who could not resist had generally done less well.

The interesting part is what the successful children actually did. Mischel observed that the children who stared at the marshmallow, picked it up or smelt it always ended up eating it. The ones who managed to resist looked away, covered their eyes or sang to themselves. They were not making a greater effort; they were removing the need to make one at all.

Mischel then proved something more useful. When he taught a new group of children one simple technique — imagine it is only a picture of a marshmallow — nearly all of them succeeded in waiting. Self-control, then, is not a fixed ability that some people are born with. It is a technique, and it can be taught.

items.s: The children were promised two marshmallows if they waited.
Most of the children waited the full fifteen minutes.
The researchers went back to the same people years later.
The children who looked at the marshmallow usually managed to resist it.
According to the text, the successful children were making a bigger effort than the others.
Mischel showed that the technique could be taught to other children.

write.q: Write about a challenge you took on. Use could or was able to for the background, managed to or succeeded in for the difficult part, and couldn’t for what went wrong at first.
plan: how you managed it in the end
write.model: Two years ago I decided to learn to swim properly. I could already stay above the water, but I had never been able to breathe correctly, so I couldn’t do more than twenty metres. At first I couldn’t even get the head movement right, and I gave in twice. Then an instructor showed me one small technique: count the strokes and breathe on every third one. Within a month I managed to swim five hundred metres without stopping, and last summer I succeeded in swimming across the lake. It wasn’t strength. It was one technique.

speak.q: Talk for about a minute about something you managed to do that you thought you could not. Say what you couldn’t do at first, and what changed.
speak.model: I’ve always been able to stay above the water, but I could never breathe properly, so I couldn’t swim more than twenty metres. At first I gave in twice. Then an instructor gave me one technique — breathe on every third stroke — and within a month I managed five hundred metres. Last summer I succeeded in swimming across the lake.
